content: 1. Methscopolamine may reduce the levels of thiothixene by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. Methscopolamine also decreases thiothixene levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism, while thiothixene may enhance the effects of methscopolamine via pharmacodynamic synergism. Close monitoring is advised due to potential additive anticholinergic effects and the risk of hypoglycemia. 2. Methscopolamine and tiotropium both reduce cholinergic effects or transmission. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 3. Methscopolamine and tolterodine both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Methscopolamine and trazodone both reduce cholinergic effects or transmission. Caution is recommended, and close monitoring is required. 5. Methscopolamine may lower the levels of trifluoperazine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Methscopolamine also reduces trifluoperazine levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism, while trifluoperazine may increase the effects of methscopolamine via pharmacodynamic synergism. Use caution and monitor closely due to additive anticholinergic effects and the potential for hypoglycemia. 6. Methscopolamine and trihexyphenidyl both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. There is a potential for additive anticholinergic effects. 7. Methscopolamine and trimipramine both reduce cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Methscopolamine and trospium chloride both decrease cholinergic effects or transmission. Caution is recommended, and close monitoring is required. 9. Methscopolamine and umeclidinium bromide both reduce cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. If possible, avoid the coadministration of additional anticholinergic agents. Serious interactions may occur, and alternative drugs should be considered. 10. Methscopolamine and umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol inhaled may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Concomitant use with other anticholinergic-containing drugs may lead to additive anticholinergic adverse effects. Close monitoring is necessary. 11. Methscopolamine and vecuronium both reduce cholinergic effects or transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Methscopolamine may decrease the levels of ziprasidone by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Methscopolamine also reduces ziprasidone levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism, while ziprasidone may enhance the effects of methscopolamine via pharmacodynamic synergism. Use caution and monitor closely due to additive anticholinergic effects and the potential for hypoglycemia. 13. Methscopolamine may lower the levels of zotepine by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction is relevant only when both agents are administered orally. Methscopolamine also decreases zotepine levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Potential adverse effects of methscopolamine include allergic reactions, blurred vision, cycloplegia, mydriasis, headache, dizziness, drowsiness, palpitations, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, taste loss, and urinary retention. Hypersensitivity to methscopolamine or related compounds may occur. Contraindications include closed-angle glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, cardiovascular instability due to hemorrhage, paralytic ileus, intestinal atony in elderly or debilitated patients, obstructive uropathy, toxic megacolon, gastrointestinal obstruction, tachycardia secondary to cardiac insufficiency or thyrotoxicosis, renal or hepatic impairment, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), congestive heart failure (CHF), coronary artery disease (CAD), hypertension (HTN), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hiatal hernia, reflux esophagitis, mitral stenosis, brain damage or spastic paralysis in children, salivary secretion disorders, Down syndrome, autonomic neuropathy, hyperthyroidism, tachyarrhythmia, and toxin-mediated diarrhea. 15. Elderly patients are at increased risk (refer to Beers Criteria) and may experience heat prostration in high environmental temperatures. Methscopolamine may cause drowsiness or blurred vision, so caution is advised when performing hazardous tasks. Use a low dosage in patients with increased susceptibility to adverse antimuscarinic effects. 16. Methscopolamine is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It is not known whether it is secreted in breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. 17. Methscopolamine reduces the volume and total acid content of gastric secretions, decreases gastric secretion, and inhibits salivation. It acts peripherally by blocking muscarinic receptors. Absorption is incomplete, with an onset of action of approximately 1 hour and a duration of 4–6 hours. Excretion occurs via urine and unabsorbed drug in feces. 18.
